chrome.footerTagline: Build apps and automate work with your own models and connected tools.

home.metaTitle: Codewhale: build with your models and tools
home.metaDescription: Build apps, automate workflows, and work across connected tools with Codewhale. Open source, with your own model APIs or local and self-hosted inference.
home.heroTitle: Build apps and automate your work.
home.heroIntro: {brand} is an open-source agent that writes code, runs commands and works with the tools you connect. Use your existing model APIs, or run models locally and on your own servers.
home.screenshotAlt: Codewhale v{version}: a captured terminal view with the conversation, message composer and session controls.
home.gainLede: Describe what you want to build or automate. Codewhale can edit files, run commands and check the result, with access you control.
gain: Create an app, add a feature or write a script. Codewhale can work through the project files, run the code and test what it builds.
Run workflows from your terminal, scripts or CI. For larger tasks, delegate parts of the work to a Fleet of agents with different models.
Add tools through plugins and MCP servers, or use APIs from your own scripts. Each service needs its own setup and authentication.
home.modelsBody: Connect your provider accounts, an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or local and self-hosted models. Pick a model for the session and for each agent in a Fleet.
modelsFacts: Connect providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or DeepSeek with your own keys.
Use an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and choose the models it serves.
Run local or self-hosted models with Ollama, vLLM or SGLang.
home.startLede: Install Codewhale, connect a model and open a project folder. You can add plugins and more agents as you need them.
home.availabilityLede: The terminal and local browser client are available now. A native desktop app and a rebuilt hosted web app are in development.
availability: Install on Linux, macOS, or Windows, then run codewhale, or codewhale web for the local browser client. npm and Cargo also work; Android on Termux is a preview.
A separate, community-maintained project: chat, threads, and file changes in a VS Code sidebar over the same Codewhale Runtime. Install it from the VS Code Marketplace.
Being rebuilt to match the desktop app. Today you can sign in, then type /rc in a running terminal session to continue it on the web; hosted task execution is still being qualified.
The native app becoming the main Codewhale client: folders, conversations, and model connections in one window. No public download yet.
Hosted computers that run your tasks.
home.availabilityNote: The terminal, local browser, and GUI need no Codewhale account. Hosted web and desktop use an account. When you use your own provider key, your provider bills that usage.
surfaces: Create files, run commands, inspect data and test what you build. You set the working folder and permissions.
Add skills and tools through plugins and MCP. Review and enable the connections you want the agent to use.
Use browser tools and the Computer Use plugin for work in apps and websites, with the access you grant.
Keep the conversation, tool results and work history together. Resume the task in the terminal or its local browser client.
Use Fleet to split a larger job between agents with different roles and models, and follow their progress in one place.
home.communityBody: Report a bug, improve the docs or contribute code on GitHub. You can also build plugins and share workflows with others.

docs-hooks.metaTitle: Run commands on events · Codewhale Docs
docs-hooks.metaDescription: Run your own scripts when a session starts, before a tool call, when a turn ends, or when Codewhale is waiting for you — to add context, enforce a rule, or get notified.
docs-hooks.title: Run commands on events
docs-hooks.lede: Hooks run a command of yours at set moments in a Codewhale session. Use them to block a risky command, add context to a message, log what happened, or get told when Codewhale is waiting for you.

blocks.p: Hooks live in `~/.codewhale/config.toml`. This one prints a line whenever a session starts:

blocks.code:
[hooks]
enabled = true

[[hooks.hooks]]
name = "announce"
event = "session_start"
command = "echo 'Codewhale session started'"

blocks.p: Start a session, then run `/hooks` to see every configured hook, whether hooks are on, and any entry that was rejected. `/hooks events` lists the event names.

sections.title: Block a command before it runs

blocks.p: A `tool_call_before` hook sees each tool call before it executes and can allow it, deny it, or force an approval prompt. This one refuses force-pushes. Save the script and make it executable:

blocks.code:
#!/bin/sh
# ~/.codewhale/hooks/no-force-push.sh
case "$DEEPSEEK_TOOL_ARGS" in
  *"push --force"*|*"push -f"*)
    echo '{"decision": "deny", "reason": "Force-push is blocked by a hook."}' ;;
esac
exit 0

[[hooks.hooks]]
name = "no-force-push"
event = "tool_call_before"
command = "~/.codewhale/hooks/no-force-push.sh"
condition = { type = "tool_name", name = "bash" }

blocks.p: The hook reads the call from environment variables and answers with JSON on standard output: `allow`, `deny`, or `ask`, plus an optional `reason`, a rewritten input (`updatedInput`), or extra context for the model (`additionalContext`). Exit code 2 always denies. When several hooks answer, deny beats ask, and ask beats allow.

blocks.note: `ask` forces a prompt in Ask and Auto-Review. Full Access never shows approval prompts, so there `ask` does not add one.

blocks.p: Three events can change what happens next. The rest only observe; their output is ignored and a failure is a warning.

rows: Before your message reaches the model. Can replace the text or block it.
Before each tool call. Can allow, deny, ask, rewrite the input, or add context.
Before each shell command. Can add environment variables.
When a session opens or closes cleanly.
After a turn finishes, with its status, duration, and token usage.
After each tool result, with its exit code when there is one.
When Codewhale starts waiting for an approval, an answer, or a paused goal.
When the session settles or starts working again.
When a turn fails for good, or on any error or failed tool.
When you switch between Plan, Work, and Operate.
When a sub-agent starts or finishes.

blocks.p: A `condition` narrows when a hook fires: by tool name (with `*` globs), tool category, mode, or exit code, and combinations with `all` and `any`. A condition that can never match its event is rejected when the config loads, so a gate you think is armed never sits silently inert.

rows: How long the hook may run. Default 30.
`true` (default): a failing hook only warns. `false`: the failure blocks.
`true` runs the hook as an observer only; it cannot block or rewrite.
Under `[hooks]`: where hooks run. Default: the session's workspace.

blocks.note: `[hooks] default_timeout_secs` replaces every hook's own `timeout_secs`, not just the missing ones. Leave it unset if you want per-hook timeouts.

blocks.p: A repository can include hooks in `.codewhale/hooks.toml`. Because they run commands on your machine, they load only after you trust the workspace and approve that exact file:

blocks.code:
/hooks review
/hooks approve <digest>
/hooks revoke

blocks.p: `/hooks review` shows the commands and a digest of the file; approving that digest enables those exact bytes from the next session. Any change to the file needs a new approval. Review the scripts the commands call, too.

sections.title: Use hooks in scripts and CI

blocks.p: Hooks run in the interactive session. `codewhale exec` fires none by default; add `--hooks` to fire `tool_call_before` and `shell_env`. With no one to answer, an `ask` becomes a deny.

blocks.code: codewhale exec --auto --hooks "run the test suite and fix the first failure"

docs-troubleshooting.metaDescription: Diagnose Codewhale in one command, then fix the common problems: command not found, no reply, a rejected key, network errors, a stuck turn, a session that will not resume, and MCP servers.
docs-troubleshooting.title: Fix a problem
docs-troubleshooting.lede: Start with one diagnostic command, then find your symptom below. Each fix names the exact message you will see.

blocks.code:
codewhale --version
codewhale doctor
codewhale doctor --probe-api                  # one real test call to your provider
codewhale auth status --provider deepseek     # which key is in use

blocks.p: `codewhale doctor --json` produces a diagnostics bundle without secrets, ready to attach to an issue. Plain `doctor` does not tell you which key is active and exits successfully even with no key; use `auth status` for that.

rows: `~/.local/bin` is not on your PATH in this terminal. Add `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"` to your shell profile and open a new terminal.
Your Node install is owned by the system. Do not use sudo: point npm at a folder you own with `npm config set prefix "$HOME/.npm-global"`, add its `bin` to your PATH, and install again.
A different version is already there. Run `codewhale update`, or remove the old binaries first.
The download was corrupted or altered, and nothing was installed. Try again; if it repeats, do not use a mirror.
You installed with npm, Cargo, or Homebrew. Update with that tool, for example `npm install -g codewhale`.

sections.title: No reply, or the key is rejected

rows: Your message appears but nothing answers
No key is configured, and v0.10.0 does not warn you. Press F3, choose your provider, and paste the key.
No key anywhere. Save one with `codewhale auth set --provider <name>`.
The key is wrong or revoked. Run `auth status` to see which source is used — a saved key beats an environment variable — then save the right key or `codewhale auth clear --provider <name>`.

Usually no connection to the provider. Check with `curl -sI https://api.deepseek.com` (a 401 means it is reachable). Behind a proxy, export `HTTPS_PROXY`. On Windows or strict proxies, try `CODEWHALE_FORCE_HTTP1=1`.

list: Press Esc to cancel the turn. Esc also closes menus first, so press it again if a menu was open.
If a long shell command is holding the turn, press Ctrl-B to move it into the background. The turn continues, and `/jobs` shows the command.
`/retry` sends the last request again.

blocks.p: For a detailed record, start Codewhale with `RUST_LOG=codewhale_tui=debug` (or `RUST_LOG=codewhale_tui::client=debug` for connection retries). Logs are written to `~/.codewhale/logs/`.

blocks.code:
codewhale sessions            # list saved sessions
codewhale resume <id>         # an id or a unique prefix
codewhale -c                  # the latest session in this folder

blocks.p: Inside Codewhale, Ctrl-R opens the session picker. `No saved sessions found for workspace` after `codewhale exec --continue` means the earlier run was a plain `exec`, which is not saved; use `--output-format stream-json` for runs you want to continue.
Messages you send while offline wait in a queue, saved with the session. `/queue list` shows them. When the connection is back, open one with `/queue edit <n>` and press Enter to send it.

list: After changing `mcp.json` or a server's credentials, run `/mcp reload`. `/mcp validate` only refreshes what you see.
Run the server's command yourself in a shell to confirm it starts.
If the config file is missing or broken, `codewhale mcp init --force` writes a fresh one.

blocks.code:
docker volume create codewhale-home
docker run --rm -it \
  -e DEEPSEEK_API_KEY="$DEEPSEEK_API_KEY" \
  -v codewhale-home:/home/codewhale/.codewhale \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace" -w /workspace \
  ghcr.io/codewhale-hq/codewhale:latest

blocks.p: The image runs as a non-root user and keeps your settings and sessions in the named volume. Pin a release tag instead of `latest` for repeatable setups, use one volume per project, and never bake keys into an image.

docs-configuration.metaDescription: Find Codewhale's config file, change a setting from the session or the shell, try one for a single run, and see what a repository is allowed to override.
docs-configuration.title: Change settings
docs-configuration.lede: Most settings can be changed without opening a file: from the session with `/config`, or from the shell with `codewhale config`. This page shows where settings live, how to change them, and what a repository can and cannot change for you.

blocks.p: Your settings live in `~/.codewhale/config.toml`. Print the exact path, or open the file in your editor:

blocks.code:
codewhale config path
codewhale config edit

blocks.p: To use a different file, pass `--config <path>` or set `CODEWHALE_CONFIG_PATH`; the flag wins when both are set. Codewhale was once called DeepSeek-TUI: if only an old `~/.deepseek/` folder exists, it is still read, and new settings are always written to `~/.codewhale/`.

Inside a session, `/config` opens the settings editor and `/settings` opens the settings screen. `/config audit` lists which settings can change in this session, which can be saved, and which only take effect after a restart — check it before editing by hand.
From the shell:

blocks.code:
codewhale config get tools
codewhale config set telemetry false
codewhale config unset telemetry
codewhale config dump       # the settings in effect, secrets redacted
codewhale config doctor     # unknown keys, empty secrets, malformed URLs

blocks.p: `config set` handles its named keys; for anything else it tells you which TOML table to edit instead of guessing.

sections.title: Try a setting for one run

blocks.p: `--set KEY=VALUE` changes a setting for one launch and saves nothing. It accepts `provider`, `model`, `verbosity`, `approval_policy`, `sandbox_mode`, and `telemetry`, and can be repeated.

blocks.code: codewhale --set model=deepseek-v4-pro --set sandbox_mode=read-only

blocks.p: A repository can include `.codewhale/config.toml` to suggest settings to everyone who works in it. Only a few keys are honored, and safety settings can only get stricter:

rows: The default model for this repository.
For example `"high"` for a complex codebase.
`false` turns shell commands off; `true` is ignored.

blocks.p: Keys, endpoints, provider choice, MCP servers, hooks, skills, and extra instruction files always come from your own config, so a cloned repository cannot point Codewhale at its own server or files. Start with `--no-project-config` to ignore a repository's file for one launch.
Project instructions — how an agent should work in this repository — belong in `AGENTS.md` instead. Run `/init` to create one.

docs-fleet.metaDescription: Save roles and models in a Fleet, write a repeatable Workflow, run it as a Lane you can watch and stop, and run batches of tasks with durable workers.
docs-fleet.title: Run a workflow
docs-fleet.lede: For most multi-step work you only need to ask: in Operate, Codewhale plans the steps and runs independent ones in parallel. Write a Workflow when you want the same ordered plan every time — phases, parallel branches, and a summary — with a record of each run.

blocks.p: Your Fleet is the list of roles Codewhale can hand work to, and the model each role uses. Set it up once inside a session:

blocks.code:
/fleet setup
/fleet
/fleet saved

blocks.p: `/fleet setup` walks you through a role, its model (or “use the session's model”), and where to save it: this project, or your personal profile for every repository. You review the exact file before it is written. `/fleet` shows the members of the selected Fleet, and `/fleet saved` switches between named Fleets.
A Fleet only chooses who does the work. What a worker may read, write, or run still comes from your workspace trust, [approval setting](/docs/modes), and sandbox.

A Workflow is a JavaScript file in your repository's `workflows/` folder. It describes steps; it does not do the work itself. This one reviews two areas in parallel, then combines the findings. Save it as `workflows/docs_readiness.workflow.js`:

Steps can be `agent`, `branch`, `sequence`, `reduce`, `loop_until`, `cond`, `expand`, and `teacher_review`. A workflow file has no file, shell, or network access of its own, and `import`, `fetch`, `eval`, and `async` are rejected. The agents it starts do the real work, under your normal permissions.

blocks.note: One run can start up to 1,000 agents, with at most 16 working at once; the rest wait for a slot. Loops must declare `max_iterations`.

blocks.code:
codewhale workflow run docs-readiness --runtime inline
codewhale workflow run docs-readiness --goal "prepare the 1.2 release" --verify

blocks.p: Codewhale finds `workflows/docs_readiness.workflow.js` from the name, checks it, and starts it. `--runtime inline` runs it in this terminal. The default, `tmux`, runs it in a detached tmux session that keeps going after you close the terminal. `--verify` runs the verification gates after a successful finish, and `--fleet <name>` uses a named Fleet instead of the built-in roles.
To keep the work off your checkout, add `--worktree-repo . --branch <name>`: the run gets its own git worktree and branch.
Inside a session, `/workflow` starts a workflow and `/workflows` lists or cancels the runs in that session.
Each run is a Lane. Lanes are saved to disk, so you can check on them from any terminal:

blocks.code:
codewhale lane list
codewhale lane status <lane-id>
codewhale lane logs <lane-id>
codewhale lane attach <lane-id>
codewhale lane interrupt <lane-id>

blocks.p: `lane list`, `lane status`, and `lane interrupt` accept `--json` and print a machine-readable receipt. In a session, `/lane` offers the same controls with the same results.

When you have a list of separate tasks rather than one plan, write them as a task file and run them as a Fleet run. Each task names its goal, its role, and the paths it may write. [The tutorial](https://github.com/codewhale-hq/CodeWhale/blob/main/docs/FLEET_WORKFLOW_TUTORIAL.md) has a complete `tasks.json`.

blocks.code:
codewhale fleet init
codewhale fleet run tasks.json --max-workers 4
codewhale fleet status
codewhale fleet logs <worker-id>
codewhale fleet resume <run-id>
codewhale fleet stop --all

blocks.p: `fleet status` counts queued, running, finished, and failed work from this workspace's run record. `fleet resume` picks a run back up after the laptop slept or the manager exited, without starting a new one. For the agents attached to your current session only, use `/fleet workers` (or `/subagents`).

docs-mcp.metaTitle: Connect tools with MCP · Codewhale Docs
docs-mcp.metaDescription: Add Model Context Protocol servers so Codewhale can use more tools, sign in to remote servers, run Codewhale itself as an MCP server, and try code mode.
docs-mcp.title: Connect tools with MCP
docs-mcp.lede: MCP servers give Codewhale more tools — a database, an issue tracker, a browser. Add a local server that Codewhale starts for you, or a remote server by URL. Its tools then go through the same approvals as built-in ones.

blocks.code:
codewhale mcp add git --command "uvx" --arg "mcp-server-git"
codewhale mcp add docs --url "https://example.com/mcp"
codewhale mcp list
codewhale mcp validate

blocks.p: `--command` starts a local server over stdio; repeat `--arg` for each argument. `--url` connects to a remote server over Streamable HTTP, with legacy SSE as a fallback. `mcp validate` checks the config and the servers you require.

Inside a session, `/mcp` opens the MCP manager: each server's state, transport, timeouts, errors, and discovered tools. The same actions are available there, for example `/mcp add stdio <name> <command>` and `/mcp add http <name> <url>`.

blocks.note: An MCP server runs with your permissions. Add only servers you trust, as you would any program you install.

sections.title: Sign in to a remote server

blocks.p: For a server that uses OAuth, add it by URL and log in. For a bearer token, keep the token in an environment variable instead of the config file:

blocks.code:
codewhale mcp login docs
codewhale mcp add tracker --url "https://example.com/mcp" --bearer-token-env-var TRACKER_TOKEN

blocks.p: An explicit Authorization header always wins: headers from config apply first, then the bearer-token variable, then a stored OAuth login. `codewhale mcp logout <name>` removes the stored login on this machine; the provider may keep its own grant until you revoke it there.
Servers live in `~/.codewhale/mcp.json`. `codewhale mcp init` writes a starter file. The `mcpServers` key used by other clients works too, so you can paste an existing entry.
After editing the file, run `/mcp reload` in the session; no restart is needed. A server starts only when a turn needs one of its tools, unless you mark it `"required": true` to connect at startup.

Each tool appears to the model as `mcp_<server>_<tool>`: a server named `git` with a `status` tool becomes `mcp_git_status`. `codewhale mcp tools <server>` lists what a server offers. A server that fails to connect or is disabled never shows up as an available tool.

MCP tools follow your [approval setting](/docs/modes): listing and reading a server's resources and prompts can run without a prompt when policy allows, and tools with side effects ask first. Full Access does not override repository rules or managed policy.

sections.title: Run Codewhale as an MCP server

blocks.p: Other MCP clients — including another Codewhale session — can use Codewhale's tools. Register it once:

blocks.code:
codewhale mcp add-self
codewhale mcp tools codewhale

blocks.p: `add-self` writes an entry that runs `codewhale serve --mcp` over stdio. Each client starts its own process; no network port is opened. `codewhale serve --http` is a different thing — the [Runtime API](/docs/runtime-api) for apps.

sections.title: Compose tool calls with code mode (experimental)

blocks.p: Code mode lets the model write one short JavaScript program that calls several tools, loops, and filters results, instead of making each call as a separate step. Only the program's final value goes back to the model, which keeps long lookups compact. It is on by default — `execute_tools` is advertised from the first request — and MCP and plugin tools compose inside a program the same way built-in ones do. To turn it off for one session, or in config:

blocks.code:
codewhale --disable code_mode

# ~/.codewhale/config.toml
[features]
code_mode = false

list: Nested native, MCP and plugin calls pass the same gate as a direct call: allow/deny lists, ask-rules, and review still apply. A call that needs approval raises the normal approval card and pauses the program; allow resumes it, deny fails only that call. Approving the program itself grants nothing.
MCP calls run through the session's MCP pool, and plugin tools are callable inside a program just like built-in ones.

Limits per program: 50 nested calls, 4 at a time, and 16 KiB returned. There is no fixed 30-second cap: a program runs on the turn's remaining wall clock, unbounded unless `[tui].turn_wall_clock_secs` is set.
Code mode is not available in Plan mode.

docs-modes.metaTitle: Set modes and approvals · Codewhale Docs
docs-modes.metaDescription: Choose Plan, Work, or Operate for the kind of work, and Ask, Auto-Review, or Full Access for how often Codewhale stops to ask you.
docs-modes.title: Set modes and approvals
docs-modes.lede: Two separate controls decide what Codewhale does on its own. The mode sets the kind of work — look, change, or coordinate. The approval setting decides when it stops to ask you. Change either one from the keyboard at any time between turns.

rows: Look and plan only. Codewhale can read the workspace and research, but it cannot edit files or run shell commands. Use it to understand a codebase or agree on an approach first.
Everyday coding. Codewhale reads, edits, and runs commands, within the approval setting you chose. This is the default.
Larger goals. Same permissions as Work, but Codewhale plans named steps, hands independent steps to sub-agents in parallel, and checks each result before it reports done.

blocks.p: Press Tab with an empty composer to cycle Plan → Work → Operate, or type `/mode` to open the picker. You can also switch directly:

blocks.code:
/mode plan
/mode work
/mode operate

blocks.p: The mode you pick becomes the mode your next session starts in. Codewhale refuses mode changes while a turn is running; press Esc to stop the turn first.
Press Shift+Tab to cycle Ask → Auto-Review → Full Access. Plan is always read-only, whatever you pick here.

rows: The default. File edits inside the workspace are applied and shown to you as a diff. Shell commands and other consequential tools stop for your approval.

Never stops to ask. Calls that are provably safe run. Publishing and destructive background actions are always blocked. Anything else gets one independent model review; high-risk calls and failed reviews are denied, not run.
No approval prompts. Repository rules and managed policy still block what they block. Use it only in a workspace you trust.

blocks.note: Ask applies workspace file edits without asking. Commit or stash anything you care about before you start, and use [Review what changed](/docs/review) to check or roll back edits.

blocks.p: When Codewhale stops at an approval, it shows the exact command. Answer with one key:

rows: Allow it for the rest of this session.
Deny it. Codewhale is told the call was refused.

blocks.p: The highlighted option on a new prompt is Deny, so pressing Enter without reading refuses the call. To change that, or to deny prompts that wait too long, set it in `~/.codewhale/config.toml`:

blocks.code:
[approval]
default_selection = "allow_once"   # default: "deny"
timeout_seconds = 300              # default: wait indefinitely

docs-runtime-api.metaTitle: Automate with the Runtime API · Codewhale Docs
docs-runtime-api.metaDescription: Drive Codewhale from your own scripts and apps: run one-shot prompts in CI, or start the local HTTP API and send turns, stream events, and answer approvals.
docs-runtime-api.title: Automate with the Runtime API
docs-runtime-api.lede: Scripts and apps can drive the same engine you use in the terminal. For a single job, use `codewhale exec`. For an app that needs threads, live events, and approvals, run the local Runtime API. Everything runs on your machine; there is no hosted relay.

sections.title: Run one job from a script

blocks.code:
codewhale exec "Reply with exactly: pong"
codewhale exec --auto "fix the failing test and run it again"
codewhale exec --auto --output-format stream-json "update the changelog"

blocks.p: Plain `exec` answers once without tools. `--auto` lets it use tools and approves them automatically, so use it only in a repository or container you trust; it never widens the [sandbox](/docs/sandbox). `--output-format stream-json` prints one JSON event per line and saves the session so `--continue` can pick it up. `--max-turns` and `--allowed-tools` put limits on a run.

blocks.code:
export CODEWHALE_RUNTIME_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
codewhale app-server --http            # http://127.0.0.1:7878

blocks.p: Set the token yourself before starting; if you do not, Codewhale generates one for the process and does not print it. Every `/v1/*` request must send it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. `--port` changes the port.

sections.title: Send a turn and watch it

blocks.code:
API=http://127.0.0.1:7878
AUTH="Authorization: Bearer $CODEWHALE_RUNTIME_TOKEN"

THREAD=$(curl -s -X POST "$API/v1/threads" -H "$AUTH" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{}' | jq -r .id)

curl -s -X POST "$API/v1/threads/$THREAD/turns" -H "$AUTH" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"prompt": "Summarize README.md"}'

curl -N "$API/v1/threads/$THREAD/events?since_seq=0" -H "$AUTH"

blocks.p: A thread is a conversation; a turn is one request and everything Codewhale does for it. The events stream replays from the sequence number you give and then stays open for new events, so a client that reconnects misses nothing.
[docs/RUNTIME_API.md](https://github.com/codewhale-hq/CodeWhale/blob/main/docs/RUNTIME_API.md) lists every route, request body, and event.

rows: JSON-RPC over standard input and output, with no network listener. Good for an SDK or a local probe.
Agent Client Protocol for editors such as Zed.
Offer Codewhale's tools to another MCP client. See [Connect tools with MCP](/docs/mcp).
The built-in [browser client](/docs/web), on the same API.
Health and capabilities as JSON, with no secrets.

list: The server listens on `127.0.0.1` by default. The token is a local guard, not a replacement for TLS or a VPN; do not expose the port to a network.
`--insecure-no-auth` is accepted only on a loopback address.
The API never returns your provider keys. Health and capability reports carry only metadata — no secrets, file contents, or messages.

docs-sandbox.metaTitle: Limit what commands can touch · Codewhale Docs
docs-sandbox.metaDescription: See which operating-system sandbox wraps shell commands on macOS, Linux, and Windows, turn it on where it is optional, and choose how much a command may write.
docs-sandbox.title: Limit what commands can touch
docs-sandbox.lede: Approving a command decides whether it runs. A sandbox decides what it can reach once it does. Codewhale uses the operating system's sandbox where one is available and tells you plainly when there is none.

rows: Seatbelt, automatically, when its startup check succeeds. Commands get broad read access, writes limited by the sandbox mode, and network only when the mode allows it.
Bubblewrap, automatically, once it is installed and verified working (opt out below). Without it, commands run with no OS sandbox.
No OS sandbox today. Your approval setting and Windows permissions still apply.
With `sandbox_backend = "opensandbox"`, shell commands run on an OpenSandbox-compatible service you configure; its isolation is that service's to guarantee.

blocks.p: Ask Codewhale which one it found:

blocks.code:
codewhale doctor
codewhale setup --status

blocks.p: Both report the sandbox that is actually available after your settings are applied. Codewhale never counts source code that is not wired in as a sandbox.

sections.title: Enable (or turn off) the Linux sandbox

blocks.p: Install bubblewrap — Codewhale uses it by default. To run Linux commands unwrapped instead, opt out with one line in `~/.codewhale/config.toml`:

blocks.code:
sudo apt install bubblewrap      # Fedora: dnf install bubblewrap · Arch: pacman -S bubblewrap

# ~/.codewhale/config.toml
prefer_bwrap = false

blocks.p: Codewhale uses `/usr/bin/bwrap` only when that file exists, is executable, and a probe shows it can create its sandbox namespaces — an installed-but-blocked bwrap is treated as absent, not used. Commands then see a read-only view of the system, write only where the sandbox mode allows, and have no network unless the mode enables it.

sections.title: Choose how much a command may write

blocks.code: sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"

rows: Commands can read but not write.
Commands can write inside the workspace and temporary folders, and nowhere else.
No OS sandbox. Use only on a machine or container you are prepared to lose.
You are already running inside isolation, so Codewhale adds none of its own.

blocks.p: The first two are enforced only where a sandbox is available — on Linux without bubblewrap, and on Windows, they are settings without an OS wrapper behind them. A repository's own config can make the mode stricter, never looser. For one headless run, pass `--sandbox <mode>` to `codewhale exec`; `--auto` approves tools but never widens the sandbox.

list: Availability is checked before a command starts, but the sandbox can still fail at launch because of host policy or container restrictions.
A “Permission denied” from a command is not proof that the sandbox blocked it. Codewhale labels a denial as the sandbox's only when the sandbox itself reported it.
No sandbox protects against kernel vulnerabilities or every kind of resource exhaustion.

docs-subagents.metaTitle: Run agents in parallel · Codewhale Docs
docs-subagents.metaDescription: Let Codewhale hand independent parts of a task to sub-agents, choose their roles, keep their edits in separate worktrees, and watch them work.
docs-subagents.title: Run agents in parallel
docs-subagents.lede: Codewhale can hand a focused piece of work to a sub-agent and keep going while it runs. Use this when a task splits into independent parts — mapping a codebase, reviewing a change, running tests — so they happen at the same time.

blocks.p: You do not start sub-agents with a command; you ask in plain words. In Operate, Codewhale does this on its own for independent steps. In Work, say what you want split up:

blocks.code:
Use three explore agents in parallel: one maps the auth code,
one maps the billing code, one lists the tests that cover both.
Then summarize what would break if we changed the session format.

blocks.p: Each sub-agent starts in the background and reports back when it finishes. Your composer stays free, and the parent turn picks up the results.
A role is the stance a sub-agent takes. Name one in your request, or let Codewhale choose. A sub-agent never gets more permission than your session has.

rows: Does whatever the brief says; may edit and run commands. The default.
Read-only. Maps the relevant code fast — “find every caller of this function.”
Designs an approach without changing anything.
Reads and grades a change, with a severity for each finding.
Lands one specific change with the smallest edit.
Runs tests and checks, then reports pass or fail. Does not edit code.
Short, careful second opinion on a judgment call. No commands.
Only the tools you list, for tightly limited jobs.

blocks.p: To give a role a specific model every time, save it with `/fleet setup` — see [Run a workflow](/docs/fleet).

When two sub-agents would edit the same repository, ask for each to work in its own worktree. Codewhale creates a fresh git worktree and branch for that agent beside your repository, under `.codewhale-worktrees/`, so your checkout stays clean until you merge.

A worktree is isolation, not permission: an agent that should write still needs a writing role and the paths it may change. Two agents that claim the same files are stopped before either one edits anything.

blocks.code: /subagents

blocks.p: `/subagents` (the same view as `/fleet workers`) lists the agents attached to this session and what each one is doing. Select one to read its transcript.

Sub-agents follow your [approval setting](/docs/modes). In Ask, a call that needs approval appears in your session as a normal prompt while the agent waits. In Auto-Review, each held call gets the same independent review, and nothing prompts you. Every decision you did not make yourself is written to the agent's transcript.

rows: Up to 1,024; extra launches wait for a slot.
A sub-agent may start its own, three levels deep by default, never more than eight.

blocks.p: These are ceilings, not targets. A few well-scoped agents with one clear summary beat many overlapping ones. For work that must survive a restart or a sleeping laptop, use a [Fleet run](/docs/fleet) instead.

docs-web.metaTitle: Open the browser client · Codewhale Docs
docs-web.metaDescription: Work with Codewhale in a browser tab on your own machine, or continue a running terminal session from the Codewhale web app with /rc.
docs-web.title: Open the browser client
docs-web.lede: Prefer a browser window to a terminal? Codewhale can serve its own client on your machine. It is another view of the same local session — same approvals, same sandbox, no account.

blocks.p: Run this from the folder you want Codewhale to work in:

blocks.code:
codewhale web
codewhale web --port 8788   # if 7878 is taken

blocks.p: Codewhale starts a local server at `http://127.0.0.1:7878`, prints a one-time link, and opens it in your default browser. If the browser does not open, use the printed link within ten minutes. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop; the browser session ends with it.

The browser client lists and searches your threads, shows the transcript with each tool's result, and has a composer. You can start, steer, or interrupt a turn, answer approvals, and rename or archive threads. Your provider keys stay in Codewhale; nothing is copied into browser storage.

list: The server only listens on `127.0.0.1`. There is no option to open it to your network, and it cannot run without authentication.
The link carries a single-use code, not your access token. Opening it swaps the code for a cookie tied to this process, and the code stops working.
Do not forward the port through a router, a public proxy, or a tunnel. For a phone or another machine, see the [Runtime API](/docs/runtime-api) and read its authentication rules first.

sections.title: Continue a session from the web app

blocks.p: This is different: it hands a session already running in your terminal to the signed-in Codewhale web app, so you can keep going from another device. It needs a [Codewhale account](/docs/auth#account).

blocks.code:
/rc          # in the running session; approve the one-time code in your browser
/rc status   # who controls the session now
/rc link     # print the session link
/rc stop     # hand control back to the terminal

blocks.p: While the web app holds the session, new prompts and approvals come from the browser, and the terminal stays readable. Either side can interrupt. You can also start a session this way with `codewhale rc`.

rows: Copy the printed link into a browser on the same machine within ten minutes.
That is expected. Run `codewhale web` again for a new one.
The web command does not set up providers. Check `codewhale doctor` and `/provider`.

docs-computers.metaTitle: Send a task to the cloud · Codewhale Docs
docs-computers.metaDescription: Hand a coding task to a Codewhale cloud agent through your account — quoted first, started only when you agree.
docs-computers.title: Send a task to the cloud
docs-computers.lede: A cloud agent takes a task off your machine: it works on cloud compute while you keep working locally. Nothing starts until you have seen the quote and agreed.

blocks.note: Cloud agents are a preview. A task runs through your signed-in Codewhale account, so the quote and the compute consent below apply to every task.

list: Sign in to your Codewhale account with `codewhale login`. Dispatch always runs through the signed-in account.

blocks.code: codewhale dispatch "fix the flaky login test and open a PR"

blocks.p: Codewhale shows the quoted task time for your account and asks you to agree that the repository code and any files you attach run on EU compute. Nothing starts until you agree. For scripts, pass `--yes --confirm-eu-compute` to answer both up front.
Use `--seconds` to set the task time, `--agent` to pick an Agent, and `--context-file` or `--file` to attach context.

docs-auth.metaDescription: Give Codewhale a model: save a provider key, check which key is in use, or run a local model with no key. A Codewhale account is optional.
docs-auth.title: Connect a provider
docs-auth.lede: Codewhale needs a model to answer. Save a key for a hosted provider, or point Codewhale at a model running on your own machine. You pay the provider directly; no Codewhale account is involved.

blocks.p: Get an API key from your provider, then save it. Codewhale asks for the key and does not echo it. DeepSeek is the default provider, so it is the example here.

blocks.code:
codewhale auth set --provider deepseek
codewhale auth status --provider deepseek

blocks.p: `auth status` names the source in use — config file, secret store, or environment variable — and shows only the last four characters. In a script, pipe the key in with `--api-key-stdin` instead of typing it.
You can also connect from inside Codewhale: press F3 (or type `/provider`), choose a provider, paste the key, then pick a model.

blocks.note: In v0.10.0, `auth set --provider deepseek` also switches your default model to DeepSeek Pro. Run `/model` if you want the faster, cheaper model back. Connecting through F3 keeps your current model.

blocks.p: When a key is set in more than one place, the first match in this order wins:

steps: `--api-key` on the command line, for one run.
The secret store written by `codewhale auth set`.
The provider's environment variable, such as `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`.

blocks.p: Exporting a new environment variable therefore does not replace a key you saved earlier. If a rotated key keeps failing, run `auth status` to see which source is active, then save the new key or clear the stored one:

blocks.code: codewhale auth clear --provider deepseek

blocks.p: On Linux the secret store is a private file (mode 0600) under `~/.codewhale/secrets/`, not an OS keyring. `codewhale doctor --probe-api` makes one test call to confirm that the key and the network both work.

sections.title: Use another provider or a local model

blocks.p: `codewhale auth list` shows every provider Codewhale knows and whether each one has a key. The pattern is the same for all of them: `codewhale auth set --provider <name>`, or that provider's environment variable.
Local runners — Ollama, vLLM, and SGLang — need no key by default, and your prompts stay on your machine. Start the runner, then choose it:

blocks.code:
codewhale auth list
codewhale --provider ollama --model <model-tag>

blocks.p: The [models page](/models) lists providers, local setups, and how to switch models mid-session.

sections.title: Sign in to a Codewhale account (optional)

blocks.p: A provider key and a Codewhale account are different things. The account is for account features only, such as cloud agents and continuing a session from the web app. Installing Codewhale and working locally never need one.

rows: Sign in through your browser with a one-time code.
Show which account this profile is signed in to.
List provider keys saved in your account. Values are never shown.

blocks.p: `codewhale login` does not accept provider keys; those always go through `codewhale auth set`. The session is kept in your operating system's credential manager when one is available, and in the private Codewhale secrets file otherwise — for example over SSH or in a container.

docs-trust.metaTitle: See what leaves your machine · Codewhale Docs
docs-trust.metaDescription: What stays local, what a model provider receives, what usage counting sends and how to turn it off, where the audit log lives, and how to report a vulnerability.
docs-trust.title: See what leaves your machine
docs-trust.lede: Codewhale runs on your computer and talks to the model provider you choose. This page lists what goes where, what the anonymous usage count contains, and how to switch it off — as built today.

rows: The runtime, your workspace, session history, snapshots, and the audit log.
The context each turn needs — your messages, the files and tool results Codewhale reads for that turn — goes directly to the provider you selected. There is no Codewhale relay in between.
With a local model (Ollama, vLLM, SGLang), inference never leaves your machine.
Installing and running Codewhale locally needs no Codewhale account.
Cannot edit files or run shell commands. Research it is allowed to do may still contact outside services.

blocks.p: Tools you add can send data elsewhere: an MCP server, a web search, or a hook runs with your permissions and reaches whatever it reaches. Add only ones you trust.
Codewhale counts anonymous usage by default and says so the first time you launch it, naming Codewhale and PostHog. Here is exactly what it covers:

rows: Prompts, responses, code, diffs, file contents, file or repository or branch names, paths, model ids, MCP server names, API keys or tokens, error message text, keystrokes, or any per-turn or per-tool timeline.
Version and platform classes, session length and outcome, feature and error counts as fixed categories, and a random install id that changes every 90 days.

`https://telemetry.codewhale.net/v1/telemetry`, a first-party service whose source is in the repository. It stores no IP address, country, or location, keeps no request logs, and holds data for three months.
Forwarding to PostHog happens only if the service operator configures it separately; it carries the same fields and nothing more.

blocks.code:
codewhale config set telemetry false   # stop, and erase the local id and buffer
CODEWHALE_TELEMETRY=0 codewhale        # stop for this process, erase nothing

blocks.p: The config setting is the lasting choice: later versions keep it, and a command-line flag or environment variable cannot turn it back on. You can also switch it in `/settings`. Turning it off deletes what was kept on your machine; rows already sent are keyed only to the random id you just erased, and expire with the three-month window.

To see exactly what would be sent without sending anything, set `telemetry_endpoint = ""` in `~/.codewhale/config.toml`. Each batch is then written to `$CODEWHALE_HOME/telemetry/dryrun.jsonl` on your machine, byte for byte, and no network connection is made.

Credential, approval, and elevation events are appended to `$CODEWHALE_HOME/audit.log` (by default `~/.codewhale/audit.log`). Writing is best-effort: if a write fails, the failure is logged rather than hidden. The log never leaves your machine.
Email security reports to the address below instead of opening a public issue. Include your Codewhale version (`codewhale --version`) and steps to reproduce if you have them.

computer-use.metaDescription: Download and set up Codewhale Computer Use for Mac. Background app control, permission setup, and human Pause and Stop controls.
computer-use.title: Computer Use
computer-use.lead: Let Codewhale work in your apps while you keep working. The Mac helper brings permissions, background app control, and a way to pause or stop input to your menu bar.
computer-use.downloadZip: ZIP archive (used by the in-app updater)
computer-use.requirements: macOS 13.5 or later · Apple silicon and Intel
computer-use.included: One app download. No separate Node installation or compiler required.
computer-use.pendingBody: The public installer will appear here after Apple notarization and release checks are complete.
computer-use.unavailableTitle: Download availability could not be checked
computer-use.unavailableBody: Refresh this page to try again, or check the published releases below.

steps.title: Install the app
steps.body: Open the disk image and drag Codewhale Computer Use into Applications. Open it from Applications, then choose Computer Use from the whale icon in your menu bar.

steps.title: Review permissions
steps.body: Use the setup buttons to open Accessibility and Screen Recording in System Settings. You choose which permissions to grant.

steps.title: Run the background check
steps.body: The helper opens a disposable practice window, enters text, and captures that window. It checks whether the pointer or active app changed during the run.

steps.title: Connect it to Codewhale
steps.body: Review, trust, and enable Computer Use in Codewhale’s plugin marketplace. Use plugin 0.3.1 or later so local actions go through the helper’s Pause and Stop controls.

computer-use.controlsBody: Supported actions operate on the selected app in the background. Apps and gestures that need foreground control require your authorization. The menu shows the target and input mode; Pause suspends helper input, and Stop ends its existing sessions.
computer-use.updateBody: Choose Check for updates from the app. Before installing an update, it checks the download, Codewhale signature, and Apple notarization, and keeps the previous app for recovery.
computer-use.platforms: This download is for Mac. Windows and Linux currently use the source plugin and host-side setup.
